lessons.title: Selecting High-Quality Seeds for Your Region
lessons.body:
Choosing the right tomato seed is the first step to a successful harvest. In Africa, you need varieties that tolerate heat, resist local diseases, and produce well in your specific climate. Start by identifying your agro-ecological zone: highlands (cool, wet), mid-altitude (moderate), or lowlands (hot, dry). For highlands, choose varieties like 'Moneymaker' or 'Roma' that set fruit at lower temperatures. In hot lowlands, pick heat-tolerant types such as 'Tengeru 97' or 'Pesa' from Tanzania. If you face bacterial wilt, look for grafted seeds or resistant varieties like 'MT 56'.

Always buy certified seed from a reputable agro-dealer or government research station. Avoid saving seeds from hybrid tomatoes because they won't grow true to type. Check the label for germination percentage (should be above 85%), purity (above 98%), and the production date (use within one year). For open-pollinated varieties, you can save seeds from your best plants, but ferment them first: scoop seeds into a jar, add water, let sit for 3 days, then rinse and dry.

Test germination before planting: count 10 seeds, place them on a wet paper towel, keep moist and warm (25-30Â°C). After 7-10 days, count how many sprout. If fewer than 7 germinate, buy new seed. Store seeds in a cool, dark, dry placeâa sealed jar with a desiccant packet works well. Never store in a plastic bag in the sun.

Consider seed treatments. Coating seeds with fungicide (like Thiram) reduces damping-off. For organic growers, soak seeds in hot water (50Â°C) for 25 minutes to kill seed-borne bacteria, then dry. Always wear gloves when handling treated seeds. Finally, calculate how much seed you need: about 100-150 grams per hectare for direct seeding, or 50 grams for transplanting. Buy enough for the season plus 10% extra.

lessons.title: Seed Starting Indoors: Timing and Materials
lessons.body:
Starting tomato seeds indoors gives you a head start, especially in areas with short rainy seasons. Begin 4-6 weeks before you plan to transplant to the field. In East Africa, if the long rains start in March, sow seeds in early February. In West Africa, for dry-season irrigation, sow in October for a November transplant. Use a calendar and count back from your expected last frost or first reliable rain.

You need clean containers: seedling trays, plastic cups with holes punched in the bottom, or wooden boxes. Avoid using soil from your garden because it may carry diseases and compacts easily. Instead, make your own seed-starting mix: 1 part sterilized garden soil, 1 part river sand, and 1 part well-rotted manure or compost. Sterilize soil by baking it in an oven at 180Â°C for 30 minutes or pouring boiling water over it and letting it cool. Fill containers to 1 cm from the top.

Sow seeds 0.5 cm deep, one seed per cell or 2-3 seeds in a cup, then thin to the strongest seedling. Water gently with a fine rose watering can or spray bottle until the mix is moist but not soggy. Cover trays with a plastic sheet or newspaper to keep humidity high. Keep them in a warm place (20-25Â°C) away from direct sun. Germination takes 5-10 days.

As soon as seedlings emerge, remove the cover and move them to bright lightâa sunny windowsill or a shade net structure that lets in 50% light. If light is poor, seedlings become tall and weak (leggy). Turn trays daily so stems grow straight. Water from the bottom by placing trays in a shallow pan of water for 10 minutes, then remove. This prevents damping-off. Label each variety with a waterproof marker and date. With proper timing and clean materials, you'll have strong transplants ready for the next stage.

lessons.title: Managing Temperature, Light, and Moisture for Germination
lessons.body:
Tomato seeds germinate best at 20-25Â°C. Below 15Â°C, germination is slow and uneven; above 35Â°C, seeds may die. In hot African lowlands, start seeds in the coolest part of the dayâearly morning or eveningâand place trays in a shaded nursery. In highlands, use a cold frame or greenhouse to trap warmth. You can also use a simple thermometer to monitor soil temperature. If it's too cold, place trays on a warm surface like a sunny rock or use a heated mat if available. For small-scale growers, a black plastic sheet over the soil before sowing can raise temperature by 2-3Â°C.

Light is critical after germination. Once seedlings break the surface, they need 12-16 hours of bright light daily. If growing indoors, use fluorescent tubes 5 cm above the plants, moving them up as plants grow. Outdoors, use a shade net that allows 50-70% lightâtoo much direct sun scorches young leaves, too little causes leggy stems. In areas with heavy rain, a simple polythene tunnel protects seedlings from downpours and keeps light adequate.

Moisture must be consistent. The seed-starting mix should feel like a wrung-out spongeânever dry, never waterlogged. Water with a fine mist twice daily in hot weather, once daily in cool weather. Overwatering causes damping-off, a fungal disease that rots stems at the soil line. To prevent it, ensure good drainage, avoid overcrowding, and water in the morning so leaves dry by evening. If you see white mold on the soil surface, reduce watering and increase airflow.

You can make a self-watering system using a cotton wick: place one end in a water reservoir and the other in the tray. The wick pulls water as needed. For large nurseries, use drip irrigation with a timer. Check moisture by sticking your finger 2 cm into the mix. If it's dry, water; if wet, wait. Keep a record of temperature, watering, and germination dates to learn what works best in your area.

lessons.title: Transplanting Seedlings into Larger Containers
lessons.body:
When seedlings have 2-3 true leaves (not the first two seed leaves), they need more space. Transplant them into larger containersâindividual pots, plastic bags, or seedbedsâso roots can grow without competition. This is called 'pricking out' or 'potting on'. Do it in the evening or on a cloudy day to reduce shock. Water the seedlings thoroughly a few hours before transplanting so the soil holds together.

Prepare your new containers: 8-10 cm diameter pots or 10x15 cm plastic bags with drainage holes. Use the same soil mix as before, but add a handful of well-rotted manure or a teaspoon of NPK 17:17:17 per pot. Moisten the mix. Using a small stick or pencil, make a hole in the center deep enough to bury the stem up to the first leaves. Tomatoes can be buried deeper than they were growingâthis promotes new roots along the stem.

Gently lift a seedling by its leaf (never the stem) from the seed tray. If roots are tangled, separate them carefully. Place the seedling in the hole, fill with soil, and press gently to remove air pockets. Water immediately with a dilute starter solution (1 tablespoon of NPK 17:17:17 in 10 liters of water) to reduce transplant shock. Keep the transplanted seedlings in a shaded area for 2-3 days, then gradually expose them to more sun.

Space pots 10 cm apart to allow air circulation. Water daily, but avoid wetting leaves to prevent fungal diseases. After one week, fertilize weekly with a balanced liquid fertilizer. If you see yellow lower leaves, add a little nitrogen. Seedlings are ready for the field when they are 15-20 cm tall, have a thick stem, and 5-7 true leavesâusually 4-6 weeks after sowing. Hardening off comes next.

lessons.title: Hardening Off Seedlings Before Field Planting
lessons.body:
Hardening off is the process of gradually exposing seedlings to outdoor conditions so they can survive the shock of transplanting. Without it, seedlings grown indoors or in a sheltered nursery may wilt, sunburn, or die when moved to the field. Start hardening off 7-10 days before your planned field planting date. If your seedlings were already outdoors in a shade net, you still need to reduce water and expose them to more sun and wind.

On day 1, move seedlings outside to a protected spot with morning sun and no wind for 2 hours. Bring them back indoors or under shade. On day 2, leave them out for 4 hours. Day 3: 6 hours. Day 4: 8 hours, including some direct sun. By day 7, leave them out overnight if temperatures stay above 15Â°C. If a cold spell or heavy rain is forecast, delay. In hot lowlands, avoid midday sun during hardening; use early morning and late afternoon sun instead.

Reduce watering during hardening. Let the soil dry slightly between wateringsâthis encourages roots to grow deeper and toughens the plant. But don't let them wilt completely. If leaves start to yellow or drop, you're pushing too hard; back off for a day. A dilute seaweed extract or compost tea spray can help reduce stress.

If you don't have space to move trays in and out, use a shade net that you can open and close. Start with 50% shade, then remove it gradually. Another method: place seedlings under a tree that provides dappled light, then move them to full sun after a week. Hardened seedlings have thicker stems, darker green leaves, and a stronger root system. They will establish faster and produce earlier. Always transplant in the evening or on a cloudy day, and water immediately after planting.

lessons.title: Grafting Techniques for Disease Resistance
lessons.body:
Grafting joins a tasty tomato variety (scion) onto a rootstock that resists soil-borne diseases like bacterial wilt, fusarium, and nematodes. This is especially valuable in Africa where these diseases devastate crops. You need rootstock seeds (e.g., 'Beaufort', 'Maxifort', or local resistant varieties like 'Hawaii 7996') and your preferred scion. Start rootstock seeds 5-7 days before scion seeds so stems are the same size.

Use the 'tube graft' or 'slant graft' method. When seedlings have 2-3 true leaves and stems are 2-3 mm thick, cut the rootstock stem at a 45Â° angle about 2 cm above the soil, leaving one cotyledon. Cut the scion stem at a matching angle, also 2 cm above the soil. Slide the two cut surfaces together so they interlock. Secure with a small grafting clip or a piece of aluminum foil wrapped gently. Keep the grafted plant in a humid, shaded healing chamber for 5-7 daysâa plastic tent with 90% humidity and 25Â°C works well. No direct light during this time.

After 5 days, open the chamber slightly each day to reduce humidity gradually. After 10 days, remove the clip if the graft has taken. You'll know it's successful if the scion stays green and starts growing. If it wilts, the graft failed; discard. Harden off grafted plants like normal seedlings before transplanting. Plant them with the graft union 2-3 cm above the soil line to prevent the scion from rooting and losing disease resistance.

Grafting costs more and takes skill, but it can double yields in infected fields. For smallholders, buy grafted seedlings from a reputable nursery if you can't graft yourself. Always sterilize your cutting tool with alcohol or bleach between plants to avoid spreading disease. With practice, you can produce your own grafted tomatoes and reduce losses significantly.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Seed Selection and Transplant Production for Tomato Farming in Africa

Tomato farming is one of the most profitable horticultural enterprises in Africa, but profitability begins long before the first fruit is harvested. It begins with the seed. Whether you are a smallholder producing for local markets or a commercial grower supplying supermarkets and processors, the quality of your seed and the health of your transplants determine your yield ceiling, your input costs, and your access to premium buyers. This practical reference consolidates the essential knowledge from this module into a single, business-focused guide for African tomato producers.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, tomato yields average 10â15 tonnes per hectare, compared with 40â60 tonnes per hectare in well-managed commercial systems. A significant portion of this gap is attributable to poor seed selection, weak seedling management, and inadequate hardening before transplanting. Each of these factors is within your control. This lesson provides the data, diagrams, and checklists you need to close that gap.

Table 1: Recommended Tomato Varieties by African Region and Market Segment

Variety selection should be driven by your target market, disease pressure, and climatic zone. The table below summarises proven options across major African tomato-growing regions.

Region / Country Market Segment Recommended Varieties Key Traits Maturity (days)
West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana) Fresh market (local) Padma, Roma VF, UC82B Heat tolerance, firm fruit, bacterial wilt tolerance 75â85
East Africa (Kenya, Tanzania) Supermarket / export Anna F1, Eden F1, Rambo F1 Uniform ripening, long shelf life, TYLCV resistance 70â80
Southern Africa (Zimbabwe, Zambia) Processing Heinz 1370, Roma VF, Peto 86 High soluble solids, determinate, mechanical harvest 85â95
Sahel (Senegal, Mali) Fresh market Mongal F1, F1 Mongal, local landraces Extreme heat tolerance, drought resilience 70â80
Highlands (Ethiopia, Rwanda) Fresh market / processing Marglobe, Moneymaker, Tanya F1 Cool tolerance, Fusarium resistance 80â90

Source: Compiled from AVRDCâThe World Vegetable Center (2016), Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) variety recommendations (2021), and Nigeria's National Horticultural Research Institute (NIHORT) released varieties (2020).

Table 2: Seed Starting and Transplant Production Parameters

These parameters are critical for producing uniform, vigorous transplants. Deviations increase disease risk and reduce field establishment rates.

Parameter Optimal Range Risk if Out of Range African Context Note
Germination temperature 20â25Â°C Below 15Â°C: slow, uneven; above 30Â°C: poor germination Use shaded nursery or cold frame in hot lowlands
Seedling growing temperature 18â22Â°C (day), 15â18Â°C (night) High temps cause leggy, weak stems Highland areas naturally suitable; lowlands need shade nets
Light requirement 14â16 hours light; 20,000â30,000 lux Low light causes etiolation and poor root development Supplement with LED or fluorescent in cloudy seasons
Media moisture 60â70% field capacity; not waterlogged Overwatering: damping-off; underwatering: wilting, stunting Use well-drained coco peat or sterilised soil mix
Seedling age at transplanting 25â35 days (5â7 true leaves) Older seedlings: transplant shock, early flowering Plan nursery calendar around rainfall onset
Hardening period 7â10 days No hardening: 30â50% transplant mortality Reduce water and expose to sun gradually
Graft healing conditions 25â28Â°C, 85â95% RH, shaded Failure of graft union, infection Use simple humidity chamber or polythene tunnel

Source: FAO, Good Agricultural Practices for Tomato (2019); AVRDCâThe World Vegetable Center, Tomato and Pepper Production in the Tropics (2016); and the University of Florida IFAS Extension, Tomato Transplant Production (2020).

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING: Seed Treatment and Chemical Handling

Many certified tomato seeds are sold pre-treated with fungicides (e.g., thiram, captan) or insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid). These treated seeds are toxic if ingested and can cause skin and eye irritation. Always wear gloves when handling treated seed. Never eat, drink, or smoke while handling. Store treated seed away from food, feed, and children. In Africa, where informal seed exchange is common, never assume seed is untreated â check the label or ask the supplier. If you treat seed yourself with hot water (50Â°C for 25 minutes) to control bacterial pathogens, use a calibrated thermometer and do not exceed the temperature, as this can kill the embryo. Dispose of treatment water safely; do not pour into streams or wells. For grafting, use clean, sterilised blades and wash hands with soap after handling plant sap, which can cause skin irritation in sensitive individuals.

Quick Reference Checklist: Seed Selection and Transplant Production

  • Select certified, region-adapted seed â choose varieties with resistance to local diseases (bacterial wilt, TYLCV, Fusarium) and matching your market (fresh, processing, export).
  • Verify seed quality â check germination rate (minimum 85%), purity, and expiry date. Buy from licensed agro-dealers, not open markets.
  • Start seeds indoors or in a protected nursery â use sterile media, clean trays, and sow at the correct depth (0.5â1 cm).
  • Manage temperature, light, and moisture â maintain 20â25Â°C for germination, 14â16 hours of light, and consistent moisture without waterlogging.
  • Pot up at the 2â3 true leaf stage â transplant into larger containers to prevent root binding and promote strong root systems.
  • Harden off for 7â10 days â gradually reduce water and increase sun exposure before field planting to prevent transplant shock.
  • Consider grafting â for bacterial wilt or Fusarium-prone soils, graft onto resistant rootstock and heal under high humidity and shade.
  • Transplant at the right age â 25â35 days, 5â7 true leaves, and always in the cool of the evening or on a cloudy day.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Good Agricultural Practices for Tomato (2019) â comprehensive guide covering seed selection, nursery management, and transplanting in tropical and subtropical conditions.
  • AVRDCâThe World Vegetable Center â Tomato and Pepper Production in the Tropics (2016) â detailed technical manual with region-specific variety recommendations and grafting protocols.
  • Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) â free variety descriptions, nursery guides, and disease management bulletins for East African tomato growers.
  • National Horticultural Research Institute (NIHORT), Nigeria â released tomato varieties, seed production guidelines, and training materials for West African farmers.
  • University of Florida IFAS Extension â Tomato Transplant Production (2020) â practical, research-based guidance on seedling media, temperature, and hardening.

This practical reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course on Tomato Farming, Module: Seed Selection and Transplant Production. For business planning, combine this technical guidance with market analysis and cost-of-production records to make informed decisions on variety choice and nursery investment.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important when selecting tomato seeds for a hot lowland region?
quiz.explanation: Heat tolerance is critical because high temperatures can prevent fruit set and reduce yields in lowland areas.

quiz.q: What is the recommended germination percentage for certified tomato seeds?
quiz.explanation: Certified seeds should have a germination percentage above 85% to ensure good field establishment.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid saving seeds from hybrid tomato varieties?
options: B) They won't grow true to type
quiz.explanation: Hybrid seeds are produced by crossing two parent lines, so saved seeds may not retain the desired characteristics.

quiz.q: How can you test tomato seed germination at home?
options: B) Plant them in the field
C) Use a wet paper towel
D) Put them in a fridge
quiz.explanation: Placing seeds on a wet paper towel and keeping them warm allows you to count how many sprout within 7-10 days.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of soaking tomato seeds in hot water at 50Â°C for 25 minutes?
options: C) To soften the seed coat
quiz.explanation: Hot water treatment kills bacteria like those causing bacterial spot and canker without harming the seed.

quiz.q: When should you start tomato seeds indoors if you plan to transplant in early March?
quiz.explanation: Tomato seedlings need 4-6 weeks before transplanting, so starting in early February gives them enough time to grow.

quiz.q: Which material is best for making a seed-starting mix?
options: B) 1 part soil, 1 part sand, 1 part compost
quiz.explanation: A mix of soil, sand, and compost provides good drainage, aeration, and nutrients for seedlings.

quiz.q: How deep should you sow tomato seeds in a seedling tray?
quiz.explanation: Tomato seeds are small and should be covered lightly, about 0.5 cm deep, to allow light and easy emergence.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for tomato seed germination?
quiz.explanation: Tomato seeds germinate best at 20-25Â°C; temperatures outside this range slow or prevent germination.

quiz.q: Why should you water seedlings from the bottom?
options: C) To make them grow faster
quiz.explanation: Bottom watering keeps the soil surface dry, reducing the risk of fungal diseases like damping-off.

quiz.q: What does 'leggy' mean in tomato seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Leggy seedlings have long, thin stems due to insufficient light, making them weak and prone to breakage.

quiz.q: How can you increase soil temperature for seed germination in a cold area?
options: B) Use a black plastic sheet
quiz.explanation: A black plastic sheet absorbs sunlight and raises soil temperature by 2-3Â°C, promoting faster germination.

quiz.q: What is damping-off?
options: B) A fungal disease that rots stems
quiz.explanation: Damping-off is a fungal disease that causes seedlings to rot at the soil line and collapse.

quiz.q: When are tomato seedlings ready to be transplanted into larger containers?
options: A) When they have 2-3 true leaves
C) When they are 30 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Seedlings are typically pricked out when they have 2-3 true leaves, as they need more space for root growth.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury a tomato seedling when transplanting into a larger container?
options: B) Up to the first leaves
D) Leave the stem above soil
quiz.explanation: Tomatoes can be buried up to the first leaves to encourage new roots along the buried stem.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of adding NPK 17:17:17 to the transplanting mix?
quiz.explanation: NPK 17:17:17 is a balanced fertilizer that supplies nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium for healthy growth.

quiz.q: How often should you water newly transplanted seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Newly transplanted seedlings need daily watering to establish, but avoid waterlogging.

quiz.q: What is hardening off?
options: B) Gradually exposing seedlings to outdoor conditions
quiz.explanation: Hardening off is the process of acclimating seedlings to sun, wind, and cooler temperatures before field planting.

quiz.q: How many days before field planting should you start hardening off seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Hardening off should begin 7-10 days before transplanting to give seedlings time to adjust gradually.

quiz.q: What should you do if seedlings wilt during hardening off?
options: B) Move them back to shade
quiz.explanation: Wilting indicates stress; moving them back to shade and reducing exposure time helps them recover.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of grafting tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Grafting onto resistant rootstocks protects against diseases like bacterial wilt and nematodes.

quiz.q: Which rootstock is commonly used for disease resistance in tomatoes?
quiz.explanation: Beaufort is a popular rootstock known for resistance to fusarium, verticillium, and nematodes.

quiz.q: What is the best time to graft tomato seedlings?
options: A) When stems are 2-3 mm thick
C) When they are 30 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Grafting is done when seedlings have 2-3 true leaves and stems are 2-3 mm thick for successful union.

quiz.q: How long should grafted plants stay in a healing chamber?
quiz.explanation: Grafted plants need 5-7 days in a humid, shaded chamber for the graft union to heal.

quiz.q: Why should the graft union be kept above the soil line when planting?
quiz.explanation: If the scion touches soil, it may develop its own roots and lose the disease resistance from the rootstock.

quiz.q: What tool should be sterilized between grafts?
quiz.explanation: Sterilizing the cutting blade with alcohol or bleach prevents spreading pathogens from plant to plant.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a successful graft?
options: B) Scion stays green and grows
quiz.explanation: A successful graft shows the scion remaining green and starting to grow after the healing period.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for potted seedlings after transplanting into larger containers?
quiz.explanation: Spacing pots 10 cm apart allows air circulation and prevents overcrowding, reducing disease risk.

quiz.q: How can you reduce transplant shock when moving seedlings to the field?
options: A) Transplant on a sunny day
quiz.explanation: Watering immediately after transplanting helps settle the soil around roots and reduces stress.

quiz.q: What is a good source of certified tomato seeds in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Government research stations and reputable agro-dealers provide certified seeds with known quality.
